summary: Older tricyclic antidepressant mainly used for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). Often works when other medicines fail, but has more side effects, including drowsiness, weight gain, heart rhythm changes, and sexual side effects. Carries a boxed warning about suicidality in children, teens, and young adults.
description: Clomipramine is a tricyclic antidepressant most commonly used to treat obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). It can be very effective, especially in people who have not responded to other medications, but it also tends to cause more side effects than modern SSRIs. Common problems include dry mouth, constipation, dizziness, drowsiness, weight gain, and sexual dysfunction. It can also affect heart rhythm, blood pressure, and sodium levels, and in rare cases can cause serious reactions like seizures, severe liver problems, or dangerous skin or immune reactions. Like all antidepressants, clomipramine carries an FDA boxed warning about increased suicidal thoughts and behavior in children, adolescents, and young adults, especially in the first weeks of treatment or after dose changes. Doses are usually started low and increased slowly, and the medication should be tapered gradually rather than stopped suddenly.
patient_summary: Clomipramine (brand name Anafranil) is an older antidepressant that doctors mainly use for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). It can reduce obsessive thoughts and compulsive rituals, but it often causes more side effects than newer medicines. Many people notice dry mouth, constipation, feeling sleepy or lightheaded, weight gain, and sexual side effects like trouble ejaculating or reaching orgasm. It can also affect your heart rhythm and blood pressure, so doctors check your heart and sometimes your blood work. Like other antidepressants, it can increase suicidal thoughts in some children, teens, and young adults, especially when starting or changing the dose, so close monitoring is essential. If clomipramine is helping, most people stay on it for months to years, and it should be tapered slowly with your prescriber’s guidance, not stopped suddenly.

primary.context: FDA-approved for OCD in adults and in children ≥10 years. Usually reserved for moderate to severe OCD or when SSRIs and therapy are not enough.

off_label.context: Can be used for treatment-resistant depression when first-line antidepressants fail or are not tolerated. Narrow therapeutic index and more side effects than SSRIs/SNRIs.
Sometimes used for panic disorder when other medications and CBT are not sufficient. Initiation and dose increases must be slow due to side effects and suicidality risk.

therapeutic_response.display: Mood and anxiety benefits usually begin within 1–2 weeks; full effect may take 4–12 weeks, especially for OCD.

common_adverse_effects.incidence: Very common (dry mouth up to ~60–80%, constipation ~20–50%)
common_adverse_effects.notes: Sip water frequently, chew sugar-free gum, and increase fiber and fluids. Severe constipation (no bowel movement for several days, pain, or bloating) needs medical attention.

You may feel sleepy or heavy, especially at the beginning or after dose increases. Taking the full dose at bedtime (when approved by your prescriber) can reduce daytime sedation. Avoid driving until you know how you respond.
You may feel hungrier and gain weight over months. Planning meals, watching portion sizes, and staying active can help.

common_adverse_effects.incidence: Common, especially in men (e.g., delayed ejaculation in up to ~40%)
common_adverse_effects.notes: Sexual side effects often persist while on the medicine. Don’t stop on your own; talk with your prescriber about dose adjustment or alternatives.

common_adverse_effects.effect: Orthostatic Hypotension (drop in blood pressure when standing)
common_adverse_effects.notes: You may feel lightheaded or faint when you stand up quickly. Stand up slowly, and tell your clinician if you’re having near-fainting, falls, or blackouts.

common_adverse_effects.incidence: Common (tremor reported in around one-third of patients)
common_adverse_effects.notes: A mild hand tremor or muscle twitch can occur. Worsening tremor, severe restlessness, or jerking movements should be reported.

serious_risks.risk: Suicidal thoughts or behavior, new or worse depression, or sudden extreme mood changes—especially in children, teens, and young adults. This needs urgent contact with your prescriber or emergency services.
Heart rhythm problems: fast, irregular heartbeat, chest pain, fainting, or severe dizziness—call emergency services.
Seizures: convulsions, loss of consciousness, or uncontrolled jerking movements.
Serotonin syndrome: high fever, confusion, sweating, stiff or jerking muscles, fast heart rate, diarrhea—medical emergency.
Severe allergic or immune reactions, including DRESS: fever, rash, swollen glands, facial swelling, with problems in liver, kidneys, or blood cells.
Severe skin reactions (rare): widespread rash, blistering, skin peeling, or sores in the mouth or eyes.
Low sodium (hyponatremia): confusion, severe fatigue, headache, nausea, unsteadiness, or seizures.
Severe liver injury: yellowing of skin or eyes, dark urine, severe fatigue, right upper abdominal pain.

safety.black_box_warning: Carefully monitor all patients, especially those under 25, for worsening depression, new or increased suicidal thoughts, agitation, or unusual behavior changes when starting clomipramine or changing the dose. Families and caregivers should watch closely and report concerns right away.

contraindications.contraindication: Known hypersensitivity to clomipramine, other tricyclic antidepressants, or any component of the product
Concurrent use with MAO inhibitors intended to treat psychiatric disorders, or within 14 days of stopping an MAOI
Use of clomipramine within 14 days before starting an MAOI
Starting clomipramine in a patient receiving IV methylene blue
Acute recovery phase of a recent heart attack
Use with extreme caution in patients with severe heart disease, serious arrhythmias, untreated narrow-angle glaucoma, or severe liver disease

precautions: Heart rhythm changes and blood pressure drops can occur, especially in people with existing heart disease or at higher doses.
May cause seizures, particularly at high doses or in people with a seizure history or alcohol use disorder.
Strong anticholinergic effects (severe dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, urinary retention) can be dangerous in some patients (e.g., older adults, people with prostate or bowel problems).
Risk of serotonin syndrome when combined with other serotonergic medicines (like SSRIs, SNRIs, some pain medicines, or MAOIs).
Can lower sodium (hyponatremia), especially in older adults or people taking diuretics.
TCAs, including clomipramine, are dangerous in overdose and can cause life-threatening heart rhythm problems and seizures.

interactions.interactant: MAO inhibitors (e.g., phenelzine, tranylcypromine, selegiline, isocarboxazid)
interactions.mechanism: Life-threatening reactions, including dangerously high blood pressure, serotonin syndrome, and severe nervous system effects.
interactions.action: Do NOT use together. Leave at least 14 days between stopping an MAOI and starting clomipramine, and 14 days between stopping clomipramine and starting an MAOI.

interactions.interactant: Other serotonergic medications (SSRIs, SNRIs, other TCAs, triptans, tramadol, fentanyl, lithium, St. John’s wort, tryptophan, linezolid, methylene blue)
interactions.action: Use only with careful monitoring and clear indication. Seek help immediately if you develop symptoms of serotonin syndrome.

interactions.interactant: Other medicines that affect heart rhythm (some antipsychotics, antiarrhythmics, macrolide antibiotics, fluoroquinolones)
interactions.mechanism: Increased risk of dangerous heart rhythm changes.
interactions.action: May need ECG monitoring, dose adjustments, or choosing alternative medicines.

interactions.interactant: CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, opioids, sedating antihistamines, alcohol)
interactions.mechanism: Increased sedation, dizziness, falls, and respiratory depression.
interactions.action: Use with great caution if at all. Avoid alcohol. Older adults are especially vulnerable.

interactions.interactant: Drugs that affect clomipramine metabolism (e.g., certain SSRIs that inhibit CYP2D6, smoking status changes, some antifungals, some antiepileptics)
interactions.mechanism: Levels may go up (more side effects and toxicity) or down (less benefit).
interactions.action: Prescriber may need to adjust clomipramine dose and monitor more closely, sometimes with blood level checks.

interactions.interactant: Diuretics or other medicines that lower sodium
interactions.action: Monitor sodium levels in at-risk patients, especially older adults.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: Mood and suicidality: Watch for worsening depression, new or increased suicidal thoughts, or sudden behavior changes, especially early in treatment and after dose changes.
Pulse and blood pressure: Check before and during treatment, especially in older adults and people with heart disease.
Cardiac rhythm: ECG monitoring is often recommended in older adults, those with existing heart disease, or those on other QT-prolonging drugs.
Electrolytes (especially sodium): Monitor in older adults and people at risk of hyponatremia (on diuretics, low body weight, other illnesses).
Liver function tests: Consider baseline and periodic monitoring in people with liver disease or on higher doses.
Side effects: Track anticholinergic symptoms (dry mouth, constipation, urinary issues), weight, sexual function, and cognitive changes.
Signs of serotonin syndrome: Especially when combined with other serotonergic medicines.
Adherence and discontinuation symptoms: Ask about missed doses, withdrawal-like symptoms, and recurrence of OCD or depression.

special_populations.pregnancy: Clomipramine crosses the placenta. Some data suggest a possible increased risk of certain birth defects (especially heart defects), and newborns exposed near delivery may have withdrawal symptoms (jitteriness, tremor, feeding problems, seizures). At the same time, untreated depression or OCD in pregnancy also carries significant risks. For people already doing well on clomipramine, prescribers may sometimes continue it after carefully weighing risks and benefits. For those starting treatment for the first time during pregnancy, other medications (for example certain SSRIs) are usually preferred.
special_populations.lactation: Clomipramine passes into breast milk. Most reported infants did well, but there is potential for sedation, poor feeding, or withdrawal. If used while breastfeeding, babies should be monitored for sleepiness, feeding problems, and weight gain. Other antidepressants with more lactation data are often preferred for new starts, but continuing clomipramine may be reasonable in some cases.
special_populations.pediatric: Approved for OCD in children ≥10 years. Children are more likely to have some side effects (such as vomiting, dizziness, and behavior changes). Monitoring for growth, weight, heart rhythm, and suicidality is essential. For depression in children, clomipramine is not generally used because safer alternatives exist.
special_populations.geriatric: In adults ≥65, clomipramine is generally avoided because of high risk of sedation, confusion, falls, heart rhythm changes, and low sodium. If used for severe OCD or other compelling reasons, doses must be low and increases very slow, with close monitoring.
special_populations.renal_impairment: No formal dosing guidelines exist for kidney disease, but clomipramine should be used with caution and close monitoring in people with significant renal impairment.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Because clomipramine is processed in the liver, people with liver impairment are at higher risk of side effects. Lower doses, slower titration, and periodic liver tests are recommended.

pharmacokinetics.bioavailability: About 50% due to first-pass metabolism in the liver.
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Extensively metabolized in the liver (mainly CYP2D6, with contributions from CYP1A2, CYP2C19, and CYP3A4) to desmethylclomipramine (active).
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Eliminated in urine (about half to two-thirds) and feces (about one quarter).
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Food may help with stomach upset but does not significantly change overall absorption.

dosing.titration: Dosing is highly individualized. Your prescriber will consider your age, diagnosis, other medications, liver and heart function, and history of side effects before choosing a dose. The following is a general overview—not instructions for self-treatment.

discontinuation.taper_guidance: Stopping clomipramine suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms and return of OCD, depression, or anxiety. Always work with your prescriber to taper gradually.

sections.heading: What It’s Used For
sections.text: Clomipramine is an older antidepressant that is especially useful in obsessive-compulsive disorder. It is usually not the first medicine tried, but it can be very helpful when other options haven’t worked.
items: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD): Reduces obsessive thoughts and compulsive rituals when taken consistently over weeks to months.
Treatment-resistant depression (off-label): May be used when several other antidepressants have failed, under specialist supervision.
Panic disorder (off-label): Can reduce panic attacks and anticipatory anxiety, usually together with therapy.
off_label: Panic disorder and other anxiety disorders in select cases

sections.heading: What People Often Feel

quotes: My mouth felt so dry I was always sipping water.
I was really sleepy during the day at first.
I felt a bit dizzy when I stood up too fast.
My obsessive thoughts weren’t as loud and urgent.
I still had rituals, but I could delay them and they felt less overwhelming.
It took about a month, but my mood lifted and I didn’t feel quite as trapped in my head.
It became harder to have an orgasm.
Ejaculation was delayed a lot, which was frustrating.
My sex drive dropped, even though I was less anxious.
items.note: Sexual side effects (like delayed ejaculation or difficulty reaching orgasm) are common and can be dose-related.

quotes: I was hungrier and put on some weight over a few months.
I felt tired and sluggish, especially on higher doses.
The trade-off was fewer OCD symptoms but more weight and tiredness.
items.note: Weight gain and fatigue are fairly common with long-term use.

sections.intro: Individual experiences differ, but these patterns are commonly reported:

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Clomipramine is not a quick-relief medicine. It works gradually over weeks as brain chemistry adjusts.
key_points: 1–2 weeks: Some people notice initial changes in sleep, appetite, or energy. OCD symptoms may not change much yet.
4–6 weeks: Many people begin to see clear improvement in mood and OCD symptoms.
Up to 10–12 weeks: Full benefit for OCD may take several months, especially when combined with ERP therapy.
Missed doses: Skipping doses regularly can cause symptoms to creep back and may trigger withdrawal-type symptoms.

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Across clinical trials and clinical experience, clomipramine often provides meaningful symptom reduction for people with moderate-to-severe OCD, including those who have not responded well to other medications. Benefits are greater when medication is combined with exposure and response prevention (ERP) therapy.
sections.comparison: Varies by study and comparison treatment
sections.clinical_details: Clomipramine is one of the earliest antidepressants shown to be effective in OCD, with multiple randomized trials demonstrating significant reductions in obsessive thoughts and compulsive behaviors compared to placebo. It appears to be at least as effective as SSRIs for OCD but causes more side effects and is therefore usually not first-line.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Black box warning: Antidepressants, including clomipramine, can increase suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, teens, and young adults.
sections.black_box: Carefully monitor all patients, especially those under 25, for worsening depression, new or increased suicidal thoughts, agitation, or unusual behavior changes when starting clomipramine or changing the dose. Families and caregivers should watch closely and report concerns right away.
other: Heart rhythm changes and blood pressure drops can occur, especially in people with existing heart disease or at higher doses.
May cause seizures, particularly at high doses or in people with a seizure history or alcohol use disorder.
Strong anticholinergic effects (severe dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, urinary retention) can be dangerous in some patients (e.g., older adults, people with prostate or bowel problems).
Risk of serotonin syndrome when combined with other serotonergic medicines (like SSRIs, SNRIs, some pain medicines, or MAOIs).
Can lower sodium (hyponatremia), especially in older adults or people taking diuretics.
TCAs, including clomipramine, are dangerous in overdose and can cause life-threatening heart rhythm problems and seizures.
patient_counseling: Tell someone you trust and your prescriber right away if you notice new or worse suicidal thoughts, severe anxiety, agitation, or strange behavior—especially in the first 1–2 months or after a dose change.
Get urgent help if you develop chest pain, fainting, a very fast or irregular heartbeat, severe dizziness, or shortness of breath.
Seek emergency care for signs of serotonin syndrome: high fever, sweating, fast heart rate, confusion, muscle stiffness or jerking, and diarrhea.
Avoid alcohol and other sedating drugs unless your doctor says otherwise—they can increase drowsiness and risk of falls.
Do not stop clomipramine suddenly. Work with your prescriber on a slow taper to reduce withdrawal symptoms and relapse.
Keep all medicines locked away. Clomipramine overdose is a medical emergency and can be fatal.

sections.intro: Clomipramine interacts with many other medicines. Always tell your prescriber and pharmacist about all prescription drugs, over-the-counter medicines, and supplements you use.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Stopping clomipramine suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms and return of OCD, depression, or anxiety. Always work with your prescriber to taper gradually.
key_points: Typical taper: For people taking clomipramine for ≥4 weeks, the dose is usually reduced slowly over 2–4 weeks or longer.
Long-term use: If you’ve been on clomipramine for many months, your prescriber may taper over several months to reduce withdrawal and relapse risk.
Withdrawal symptoms: Can include dizziness, headache, nausea, sweating, vivid dreams, anxiety, irritability, ‘electric shock’ sensations, and sleep problems.
If symptoms are severe: Your prescriber may increase the dose slightly again and then taper more slowly.
Do not adjust your dose on your own. Always discuss changes with your prescriber.

sections.heading: Dosing Information (Overview, Not a Prescription)
sections.text: Dosing is highly individualized. Your prescriber will consider your age, diagnosis, other medications, liver and heart function, and history of side effects before choosing a dose. The following is a general overview—not instructions for self-treatment.

adult.ocd_initial: Often starts at 25 mg once daily, usually at bedtime or divided.
adult.ocd_titration: Gradually increased over the first 2 weeks to about 100 mg/day (or up to ~3 mg/kg/day), often in divided doses at first.
adult.ocd_typical: Many adults take 100–200 mg/day. Some may need lower or higher doses depending on response and side effects.
adult.maximum: Generally 250 mg/day is considered the upper limit; higher doses are rarely used and only under specialist supervision.
adult.elderly: Lower starting doses (e.g., 10–25 mg/day) with very slow increases are used if clomipramine is considered at all, because of high risk of side effects and falls.
adult.hepatic: People with liver disease often require reduced starting doses and slower titration with careful monitoring.
adult.renal: Used with caution; no formal adjustment guidelines, but close monitoring is recommended.

sections.simple_explanation: Most people start on a low dose to check tolerance and then increase gradually over several weeks. Once a stable dose is reached and side effects are manageable, the medication is usually continued for many months if it is helping.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, and Special Groups
sections.text: Treatment decisions with clomipramine need to consider both the risks of the medicine and the risks of untreated OCD or depression.
sections.pregnancy: Clomipramine crosses the placenta. Some data suggest a possible increased risk of certain birth defects (especially heart defects), and newborns exposed near delivery may have withdrawal symptoms (jitteriness, tremor, feeding problems, seizures). At the same time, untreated depression or OCD in pregnancy also carries significant risks. For people already doing well on clomipramine, prescribers may sometimes continue it after carefully weighing risks and benefits. For those starting treatment for the first time during pregnancy, other medications (for example certain SSRIs) are usually preferred.
sections.lactation: Clomipramine passes into breast milk. Most reported infants did well, but there is potential for sedation, poor feeding, or withdrawal. If used while breastfeeding, babies should be monitored for sleepiness, feeding problems, and weight gain. Other antidepressants with more lactation data are often preferred for new starts, but continuing clomipramine may be reasonable in some cases.
sections.pediatrics: Approved for OCD in children ≥10 years. Children are more likely to have some side effects (such as vomiting, dizziness, and behavior changes). Monitoring for growth, weight, heart rhythm, and suicidality is essential. For depression in children, clomipramine is not generally used because safer alternatives exist.
sections.geriatrics: In adults ≥65, clomipramine is generally avoided because of high risk of sedation, confusion, falls, heart rhythm changes, and low sodium. If used for severe OCD or other compelling reasons, doses must be low and increases very slow, with close monitoring.
sections.hepatic: Because clomipramine is processed in the liver, people with liver impairment are at higher risk of side effects. Lower doses, slower titration, and periodic liver tests are recommended.
sections.renal: No formal dosing guidelines exist for kidney disease, but clomipramine should be used with caution and close monitoring in people with significant renal impairment.

items: Mood and suicidality: Watch for worsening depression, new or increased suicidal thoughts, or sudden behavior changes, especially early in treatment and after dose changes.
Pulse and blood pressure: Check before and during treatment, especially in older adults and people with heart disease.
Cardiac rhythm: ECG monitoring is often recommended in older adults, those with existing heart disease, or those on other QT-prolonging drugs.
Electrolytes (especially sodium): Monitor in older adults and people at risk of hyponatremia (on diuretics, low body weight, other illnesses).

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Clomipramine comes in capsule and tablet forms. Generics are widely available.
items: US: Capsules (Anafranil and generics): 25 mg, 50 mg, 75 mg
Canada: Tablets and capsules in multiple strengths (for example 10 mg, 25 mg, 50 mg, 75 mg; availability varies by brand and country)
All forms are taken by mouth; doses may be divided at first and then given once daily at bedtime after titration.

sections.heading: How It Works
sections.text: Clomipramine boosts the activity of two brain chemicals, serotonin and norepinephrine, by blocking their reuptake (reabsorption) into nerve cells. Its main OCD benefits are thought to come from strong serotonin reuptake inhibition, while its metabolite also affects norepinephrine. Over time, this helps reset overactive brain circuits involved in obsessive thoughts and compulsive behaviors. It also affects many other receptors (anticholinergic, antihistamine, and alpha-adrenergic), which explains many of its side effects such as dry mouth, constipation, drowsiness, and drops in blood pressure.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment
sections.text: For OCD and depression, newer antidepressants (especially SSRIs) are usually tried first because they are safer in overdose and have fewer side effects. Clomipramine remains an important option when OCD symptoms are severe or have not responded to several SSRIs, or when its particular profile of action is beneficial. Because of its side-effect burden and safety concerns, it is typically managed by or in consultation with a psychiatrist, with close monitoring and a careful risk–benefit discussion, especially in children, teens, pregnant patients, and older adults.

faqs.a: Clomipramine is an older antidepressant mainly used to treat obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). It can also be used in some cases of treatment-resistant depression and panic disorder when other medicines have not worked, usually under specialist care.

faqs.q: How long does clomipramine take to work for OCD?
faqs.a: Some people notice early changes in sleep or mood within 1–2 weeks, but OCD symptoms often take longer. It can take 4–6 weeks to see clear benefits and up to 10–12 weeks for full improvement, especially when combined with exposure and response prevention (ERP) therapy.

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects of clomipramine?
faqs.a: Common side effects include dry mouth, constipation, dizziness, drowsiness, blurred vision, weight gain, and sexual side effects such as delayed ejaculation or difficulty reaching orgasm. These are often dose-related. Some people also experience tremor, sweating, or trouble urinating.

Like all antidepressants, clomipramine carries an FDA boxed warning about increased suicidal thoughts and behavior in children, teens, and young adults (up to age 24), especially when starting treatment or changing the dose. It does not mean everyone will have these thoughts, but it’s critical to monitor closely and report any concerning changes to your prescriber right away.

faqs.q: Is clomipramine safe for older adults?
faqs.a: In adults age 65 and older, clomipramine is generally avoided because it can cause strong sedation, confusion, falls, heart rhythm changes, and low sodium. If it is used at all, doses must be low, increased very slowly, and monitored closely. Safer alternatives are usually preferred.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol while taking clomipramine?
faqs.a: It’s best to avoid alcohol. Alcohol can increase drowsiness, dizziness, and the risk of falls and may worsen mood symptoms. Combining alcohol with clomipramine can also impair judgment and reaction time.

faqs.q: Can I take clomipramine during pregnancy?
faqs.a: Clomipramine crosses the placenta and may be linked to some risk of birth defects and newborn withdrawal symptoms, but untreated depression or OCD in pregnancy also has serious risks. For someone already doing well on clomipramine, a prescriber may decide to continue it after careful discussion of risks and benefits. For new starts in pregnancy, other antidepressants are usually preferred. Always discuss pregnancy plans with your prescriber before changing medications.

Clomipramine passes into breast milk. In reported cases, most infants did well, but sedation, feeding problems, or withdrawal are possible. If clomipramine is used while breastfeeding, babies should be monitored closely. When starting treatment for the first time while breastfeeding, other antidepressants with more safety data are often preferred.

faqs.q: How do I stop taking clomipramine safely?
faqs.a: Do not stop clomipramine suddenly. Stopping abruptly can cause withdrawal symptoms (dizziness, headache, nausea, vivid dreams, anxiety) and risk relapse of OCD or depression. Most people should taper gradually over weeks to months, with dose reductions guided by their prescriber and adjusted if withdrawal symptoms occur.

faqs.q: Why would a doctor choose clomipramine instead of an SSRI?
faqs.a: Clomipramine is generally not first choice because of more side effects and safety concerns. However, it can be particularly effective for severe or treatment-resistant OCD. A doctor might choose clomipramine if several SSRIs have failed, were not tolerated, or helped only partially, especially when OCD symptoms are very disabling.
